headline: A last warm day in the 60s gives way to a cold, dry Tuesday and Wednesday, then a large coastal storm on Thanksgiving brings 1–2 inches of rain, east-northeast gusts of 35–45 mph (possibly 50 mph at the coast) and widespread coastal flooding.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Monday stays dry and well above normal around New York City, with highs in the 60s even as a cold front crosses in the afternoon. Record highs for the date are mostly around 70 (72 at Central Park, 74 at Newark, 70 at LaGuardia, 71 at JFK), and records look unlikely today, though Islip has tied or broken its record each of the last four days. Winds shift to the northwest behind the front with a few gusts near 23 mph this afternoon, then ease Monday night.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Tuesday and Wednesday turn much colder and stay dry as an unusually strong area of high pressure builds from the Great Lakes into the Northeast. Highs struggle to get out of the 40s, and overnight lows fall mostly below freezing, except in the New York City metro area Wednesday morning. Tuesday is sunny with northwest winds around 15–30 mph, winds turn northeast on Wednesday, and easterly winds begin to ramp up late Wednesday night.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: A much larger storm moving north along the East Coast arrives on Thanksgiving Day, slightly later than earlier forecasts; it may track inland, near or just west of the Appalachians, but strong winds are expected either way. The immediate coast may see some rain Thursday morning, with the best chance of rain Thursday afternoon into Thursday night before it tapers early Friday morning; 1–2 inches looks reasonable over about 12–18 hours, with a 20–30 percent chance of more than 2.5 inches near the coast, and flooding from rain should be limited to minor urban and poor-drainage spots because the storm moves through quickly. East-northeast winds of 20–30 mph gust 35–45 mph, possibly around 50 mph at the coast, strongest Thursday afternoon and evening, with about a 50–70 percent chance of gusts over 45 mph (advisory level) along the coast and much lower inland. Friday turns blustery with west gusts of 25–35 mph as the storm departs, and it stays breezy Saturday.

coast: Coastal flooding is growing more likely with the storm Thursday into Friday: with a full moon on the 24th and king tides this week, many locations need less than a foot of extra water to reach minor flooding, and the forecast supports widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, with localized major flooding possible in the most vulnerable spots along the South Shore back bays and western Great South Bay. Beach flooding, erosion and overwash are all possible. On the water, Small Craft Advisories run until 1 AM Tuesday for Long Island Sound east of the Connecticut River and until 1 PM Tuesday for the ocean waters, mainly for rough seas that may linger near 5 feet on the nearshore ocean into early Tuesday afternoon, with marginal advisory-level gusts possible Tuesday. After a lull late Tuesday into Wednesday, winds ramp up Wednesday night; gales are likely Thursday with possible storm-force winds Thursday and Thursday evening, and peak waves of 15–20 feet on the ocean (occasionally 20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet on Long Island Sound and around 10 feet on western Block Island Sound east of Orient Point, with gales possibly continuing into Friday.
watch_for: Widespread minor to moderate, locally major, coastal flooding with the Thanksgiving storm, helped by king tides and the full moon.
Thanksgiving winds gusting 35–45 mph, possibly 50 mph at the coast, strongest Thursday afternoon and evening.
Rain totals of 1–2 inches Thursday into early Friday, with a 20–30 percent chance of more than 2.5 inches near the coast.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in a warm Monday and a cold, dry Tuesday and Wednesday, and confidence continues in a large Thanksgiving coastal storm, though its exact track and slightly slower timing still affect the rain and wind details.
